newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela aide blasts financial markets.
newsitem.headline: Mandela aide blasts financial markets.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela's chief of staff on Tuesday criticised financial markets and called for global rules to protect developing countries from what he called "volatile unaccountability".

"The world and the developing world in particular seem to be at the total mercy of the ungovernable phenomenon of the international financial market," said Jakes Gerwel, who is cabinet secretary and head of the president's office. "One observes how the volatile unaccountability of the financial markets expresses itself seemingly in total disregard for the relevance of the government's punctilious adherence to democratic and accountable governance as well as sound fiscal policy," he said.

Gerwel made his plea during an address to the board of the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA). The prepared text was released on Tuesday after a two-day meeting of the board, which is chaired by former Commonwealth secretary general Sonny Ramphal.
Gerwel said later his remarks did not formally reflect government thinking or Mandela's personal concerns.
"I am asking, as a layman, is there anything that a government can do to be protected, or is that volatility totally beyond influence by a government's own exemplary behaviour," he told Reuters.
In the speech, Gerwel said a challenge to the concept of global governance, which IDEA seeks to promote, could be to "bring some global regularity to the world of international finance".
South Africa had made every effort since the advent of democracy in April 1994 to establish responsible government, but remained vulnerable to financial speculators, he said.

Since the transition, South Africa has failed to attract large-scale foreign capital investment and the rand has been battered by speculation since rumours that Mandela was ill triggered a slide in February.
The currency, which is still constricted by exchange controls, has lost more than 20 percent of its value since then.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who is likely to succeed Mandela in 1999, have both condemned what they call the superficial judgment of financial markets.
Gerwel warned the Stockholm-based institute's leaders that concern for democracy in developing countries had to be matched by a commitment to social rehabilitation.
"Penury is an enemy of democracy in the long run and democrats and democratic forces will have to redouble their efforts to couple the spread of democracy with socio-economic development," he said.
Gerwel said South Africa was given no credit for implementing a macro-economic strategy hailed by business and the International Monetary Fund as a model of fiscal responsibility.
